name: Genesis
author: Traditionally Moses. Most scholars think it was gathered and shaped from older sources over several centuries, reaching its final form around the time of the exile.
date: Traditionally c. 1400s BC; many scholars place its final editing c. 500s BC. It describes the time from creation to Joseph, ending perhaps c. 1700s BC.
audience: The people of Israel, who needed to know who their God was, where the world came from and why they had been chosen.
genre: Narrative (with family histories and some poetry)
storyPlace: The opening of the whole story: God creates a good world, people turn away, and God begins his rescue plan by calling Abraham and his family.
summary: Genesis tells of creation, the first sin, the flood and Babel, then follows Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph as God keeps his promise to bless the world through one family.

name: Exodus
author: Traditionally Moses. Many scholars see it as a collection of older traditions put together over time.
date: Traditionally c. 1400s BC; final form possibly c. 500s BC. The exodus itself is dated either c. 1446 BC or c. 1260 BC, and scholars debate which is right.
audience: Israel, learning the story of how God rescued them from slavery and made them his own people.
storyPlace: God rescues Abraham's descendants from slavery in Egypt, meets them at Mount Sinai and comes to live among them in the tabernacle.
summary: God calls Moses, frees Israel from Pharaoh through the plagues and the Passover, leads them through the sea and gives them his law and the plans for his tent of meeting.

name: Leviticus
author: Traditionally Moses. Many scholars link it to Israel's priests, who preserved and shaped these instructions over time.
date: Traditionally c. 1400s BC; many scholars date its final form c. 500s BC. It is set at Mount Sinai.
audience: Israel and its priests, learning how a holy God could live among an imperfect people.
storyPlace: Israel is camped at Sinai. Now that God dwells among them, they learn how to worship him, deal with sin and live as a holy people.
summary: Leviticus describes the sacrifices, the priesthood, the Day of Atonement, the festivals and everyday rules for being holy, summed up in the call to love your neighbour as yourself.

name: Numbers
author: Traditionally Moses. Many scholars think it combines older records and stories edited over time.
date: Traditionally c. 1400s BC; final form possibly c. 500s BC. It covers about forty years in the wilderness.
audience: Israel, reminded of how their ancestors' lack of trust kept them out of the land for a generation.
storyPlace: Between Sinai and the promised land: Israel wanders in the wilderness, and God stays faithful even when his people do not.
summary: Israel is counted, sets out from Sinai, refuses to enter the land out of fear, and wanders for forty years until a new generation stands ready at the edge of Canaan.

name: Deuteronomy
author: Traditionally Moses. Many scholars connect its present form with King Josiah's reforms in the 600s BC, building on older material.
date: Traditionally c. 1400s BC; many scholars date it c. 600s BC, with later additions. It is set just before Israel enters the land.
audience: A new generation of Israelites about to enter the promised land, and later readers called back to faithfulness.
storyPlace: At the end of the wilderness years, Moses renews the covenant with Israel before they cross the Jordan.
summary: Moses retells Israel's story and God's law in a series of farewell speeches, urging the people to love God with all their heart and choose life.

name: Joshua
author: Jewish tradition credits Joshua, with later additions. Scholars usually see it as part of a larger history (Deuteronomy to Kings) edited around the exile.
date: Uncertain; final form likely c. 600s–500s BC. It describes events perhaps c. 1400–1200 BC.
audience: Israel, reminded that the land was God's gift and that faithfulness to him mattered.
storyPlace: God keeps his promise to Abraham by bringing Israel into the land of Canaan under Moses' successor, Joshua.
summary: Israel crosses the Jordan, takes Jericho and other cities, divides the land among the tribes and renews its promise to serve the Lord.

name: Judges
author: Unknown. Jewish tradition suggests Samuel; scholars see it as part of the longer history edited around the time of the exile.
date: Final form likely c. 600s–500s BC. It describes the period c. 1200–1050 BC.
audience: Israel, shown what happens when a people forget God and everyone does what seems right to them.
storyPlace: After the conquest and before the kings, Israel falls into a repeating cycle of turning away, suffering, crying out and being rescued.
summary: God raises up leaders such as Deborah, Gideon and Samson to rescue Israel, but each time the people slide further into disorder.

name: Ruth
author: Unknown. Jewish tradition suggests Samuel.
date: Debated: suggestions range from c. 900s BC to after the exile. It is set in the time of the judges.
audience: Israel, shown God's quiet care and the welcome of an outsider into his people.
storyPlace: A bright story from the dark days of the judges that leads to the birth of King David's family line.
summary: Ruth, a widow from Moab, stays loyal to her mother-in-law Naomi, is welcomed by Boaz in Bethlehem and becomes the great-grandmother of David.

name: 1 Samuel
author: Unknown. Tradition links it to Samuel and the prophets Nathan and Gad; scholars see it drawn from older sources and edited around the exile.
date: Final form likely c. 600s–500s BC. It covers c. 1100–1010 BC.
audience: Israel, reflecting on how the monarchy began and what kind of king God wanted.
storyPlace: Israel moves from judges to kings: Samuel anoints Saul, Saul fails, and God chooses David.
summary: The prophet Samuel leads Israel, the people demand a king, Saul is crowned and later rejected, and the young shepherd David rises while on the run from Saul.

name: 2 Samuel
author: Unknown; originally one book with 1 Samuel and shaped from older court records and stories.
date: Final form likely c. 600s–500s BC. It covers David's reign, c. 1010–970 BC.
audience: Israel, remembering David as their great king while being honest about his failures.
storyPlace: David becomes king, and God promises that his family line will rule forever, a promise Christians see fulfilled in Jesus.
summary: David unites the tribes, makes Jerusalem his capital and receives God's covenant promise, but his sin with Bathsheba brings deep trouble to his family and kingdom.

name: 1 Kings
author: Unknown. Jewish tradition suggests Jeremiah; scholars see it as part of a history compiled from royal records around the exile.
date: Final form c. 560s–500s BC. It covers c. 970–850 BC.
audience: Israelites in or after exile, asking how they had lost their land and king.
storyPlace: Solomon builds the temple, then the kingdom splits in two, and prophets like Elijah call the people back to God.
summary: Solomon's wise and wealthy reign ends in compromise, the nation divides into Israel and Judah around 930 BC, and Elijah confronts King Ahab and the worship of Baal.

name: 2 Kings
author: Unknown; originally one book with 1 Kings.
date: Final form c. 560s–500s BC. It covers c. 850–560 BC.
audience: God's people in exile, helped to understand why disaster came and that hope remained.
storyPlace: The two kingdoms decline and fall: Israel to Assyria in 722 BC and Judah to Babylon in 587/586 BC.
summary: Elisha continues Elijah's work, a few kings like Hezekiah and Josiah seek reform, but persistent unfaithfulness ends with Jerusalem destroyed and its people taken into exile.

name: 1 Chronicles
author: Jewish tradition credits Ezra; scholars usually speak of an unknown writer called the Chronicler.
date: c. 400s–300s BC, after the return from exile. It retells history from Adam to David.
audience: Jews back in the land after exile, rebuilding their worship and identity.
storyPlace: A retelling of Israel's story from after the exile, reminding returned exiles that they still belong to God's people and to David's promise.
summary: After long family trees from Adam onward, it focuses on David's reign and his preparations for the temple and its worship.

name: 2 Chronicles
author: The same writer as 1 Chronicles, traditionally Ezra.
date: c. 400s–300s BC. It covers Solomon to the decree of Cyrus in 538 BC.
audience: Returned exiles, encouraged that God answers those who humble themselves and seek him.
storyPlace: Retells the story of Judah's kings from Solomon's temple to the exile, and ends with the hopeful decree allowing the Jews to go home.
summary: It follows Judah's kings, highlighting those who sought God and reformed worship, and closes with Cyrus of Persia inviting the exiles to rebuild the temple.

name: Ezra
author: Traditionally Ezra the priest and scribe, possibly together with the Chronicler.
date: c. 400s BC. It covers c. 538–450 BC.
audience: Jews rebuilding life in Judah under Persian rule.
genre: Narrative with official letters and lists
storyPlace: The return from exile: God's people come home, rebuild the temple and recommit to God's law.
summary: Exiles return under Zerubbabel and finish the second temple around 516 BC; decades later Ezra arrives to teach the law and call the people to faithfulness.

name: Nehemiah
author: Largely Nehemiah's own memoirs, edited together with Ezra (they were once one book).
date: c. 400s BC. It covers c. 445–430 BC.
audience: The struggling community in Jerusalem after the exile.
storyPlace: Part of the return from exile, as Jerusalem's walls are rebuilt and the covenant renewed.
summary: Nehemiah, a Jewish official in the Persian court, leads the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls despite opposition, and Ezra reads the law to the gathered people.

name: Esther
author: Unknown, probably a Jewish writer living in Persia.
date: c. 400s–300s BC. It is set in the Persian court c. 480s–470s BC. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include extra Greek passages.
audience: Jews scattered across the Persian empire, and the origin story of the festival of Purim.
storyPlace: Among the Jews who stayed in exile, God's hidden care protects his people from destruction.
summary: Esther, a Jewish woman who becomes queen of Persia, risks her life to stop a plot to wipe out her people. God is never named in the Hebrew text, yet his providence runs through it.

name: Job
author: Unknown. Some old traditions suggest Moses; the writer is anonymous.
date: Very uncertain; many scholars suggest c. 600s–400s BC. The story itself seems set in the age of the patriarchs.
audience: Anyone wrestling with suffering and the question of why bad things happen to good people.
storyPlace: Stands somewhat outside the main storyline, exploring a question every generation of God's people faces: can God be trusted in suffering?
summary: A good man loses everything, argues with friends who say he must have sinned, and finally meets God, who answers not with an explanation but with himself.

name: Psalms
author: Many writers. About half are linked to David; others to Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon, Moses and unnamed poets.
date: Written over centuries, roughly c. 1000–400 BC, and gathered into its final collection after the exile.
audience: Israel's worshipping community, for use in the temple, at home and in personal prayer.
storyPlace: The prayer book of God's people through the whole Old Testament story, from David's kingdom through exile and return, and much loved by Jesus and the early church.
summary: 150 songs and prayers of praise, lament, thanks, trust and confession that give words for every season of life with God.

name: Proverbs
author: Much of it is credited to Solomon, with sections from other wise men such as Agur and Lemuel.
date: Collected over time, from c. 900s BC to its final form perhaps c. 500s–400s BC.
audience: Young people and all of Israel, being trained to live wisely in everyday life.
storyPlace: Connected with Solomon's reign, it shows what it looks like to live well in God's world day to day.
summary: Short, memorable sayings about work, words, money, family and friendship, built on the idea that reverence for the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.

name: Ecclesiastes
author: The writer calls himself the Teacher, a son of David, traditionally Solomon. Many scholars think a later sage wrote in Solomon's voice.
date: Traditionally c. 900s BC; many scholars suggest c. 400s–200s BC.
audience: Thoughtful readers asking what life means when everything seems to pass away.
storyPlace: A wisdom book that honestly faces life's frustrations in a fallen world and points back to fearing God.
summary: The Teacher finds that pleasure, work, wealth and even wisdom cannot give lasting meaning on their own, and concludes that we should enjoy God's gifts and keep his commands.

name: Song of Songs
author: Traditionally Solomon; many scholars see it as a collection of love poems that honour or mention him.
date: Uncertain; suggestions range from c. 900s BC to after the exile.
audience: Israel, celebrating love between a man and a woman as a good gift from God.
storyPlace: A celebration of the goodness of love that God made at creation. Jews and Christians have also long read it as a picture of God's love for his people.
summary: A bride and her beloved speak of their longing and delight in each other in rich, poetic language.

name: Isaiah
author: Isaiah, a prophet in Jerusalem. Many scholars think chapters 40–66 come from his later followers during and after the exile; others hold to one author.
date: Isaiah's ministry c. 740–700 BC; later sections possibly c. 540–500 BC.
audience: Judah, facing the Assyrian threat, and later the exiles in Babylon longing for home.
storyPlace: Spans the time of the kings, the coming exile and the return, looking ahead to a servant who would suffer for others and a new heavens and new earth.
summary: Isaiah warns Judah of judgment, comforts the exiles with God's promise of rescue and paints vivid pictures of the coming king and the suffering servant that Christians see fulfilled in Jesus.

name: Jeremiah
author: The prophet Jeremiah, with help from his scribe Baruch.
date: Jeremiah's ministry c. 627–580s BC; the book was gathered during and after the exile.
audience: Judah in its final years before Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, and the first exiles.
storyPlace: The last days of the kingdom of Judah and the fall of Jerusalem, with the promise of a new covenant written on the heart.
summary: Jeremiah pleads with Judah to turn back, suffers rejection for his warnings, watches Jerusalem fall and announces that God will one day make a new covenant with his people.

name: Lamentations
author: Traditionally Jeremiah; the poems themselves do not name an author.
date: Soon after the fall of Jerusalem in 587/586 BC.
audience: Survivors grieving the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple.
storyPlace: Written at the darkest point of the Old Testament story, the fall of Jerusalem and start of the exile.
summary: Five sorrowful poems mourn the ruined city, yet at their heart they hold on to hope that God's mercies are new every morning.

name: Ezekiel
author: Ezekiel, a priest taken to Babylon with the first group of exiles.
audience: Jewish exiles in Babylon who thought God had abandoned them.
storyPlace: In the exile, God shows that his presence is not limited to the temple and promises new hearts, new life and a restored people.
summary: Through strange visions and acted-out signs, Ezekiel warns of Jerusalem's fall, sees God's glory leave the temple, and later sees dry bones come to life and a new temple filled with God's presence.

name: Daniel
author: Traditionally Daniel, an exile in Babylon. Many scholars think it was completed in the 160s BC during persecution under Antiochus IV.
date: Traditionally c. 530s BC; many scholars date it c. 165 BC. It is set c. 605–530 BC. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include extra Greek sections.
audience: Jews living under foreign powers, encouraged to stay faithful because God rules over every empire.
storyPlace: Set in the exile, it looks beyond to the rise and fall of empires and the coming everlasting kingdom of God.
summary: Daniel and his friends stay faithful in Babylon's court, surviving a fiery furnace and a lions' den, and Daniel receives visions of kingdoms rising and falling and one like a son of man receiving God's kingdom.

name: Hosea
author: The prophet Hosea.
audience: The northern kingdom of Israel in its final decades, wealthy but chasing other gods.
storyPlace: During the divided kingdom, shortly before the north fell to Assyria in 722 BC.
summary: God tells Hosea to marry and keep loving an unfaithful wife, a living picture of God's patient, faithful love for an unfaithful people.

name: Joel
author: The prophet Joel, son of Pethuel.
date: Uncertain; suggestions range from c. 800s BC to c. 400s BC.
audience: Judah, after a devastating plague of locusts.
storyPlace: Calls God's people to return to him and promises that God will pour out his Spirit on all people, a promise Peter quotes at Pentecost.
summary: A locust plague becomes a warning of the coming day of the Lord, followed by a call to repent and a promise of restoration and the gift of the Spirit.

name: Amos
author: Amos, a shepherd and fig farmer from Tekoa in Judah.
audience: The prosperous northern kingdom of Israel, where the rich were exploiting the poor.
storyPlace: During the divided kingdom, a generation before Israel's fall to Assyria.
summary: Amos warns that religious festivals mean nothing without justice, calls for justice to roll on like a river, and ends with a promise that God will rebuild David's fallen house.

name: Obadiah
author: The prophet Obadiah; nothing else is known about him.
date: Probably soon after the fall of Jerusalem in 587/586 BC.
audience: Judah, hurt by the neighbouring nation of Edom, which cheered and joined in when Jerusalem fell.
storyPlace: Around the start of the exile, promising that God sees injustice and that his kingdom will win in the end.
summary: The shortest book of the Old Testament announces judgment on proud Edom and the future restoration of God's people.

name: Jonah
author: Unknown; the book is about Jonah, a prophet from the 700s BC, rather than by him.
date: Uncertain; many scholars suggest after the exile, c. 500s–300s BC. It is set c. 780s–750s BC.
audience: Israel, challenged to see that God's mercy reaches even their enemies.
storyPlace: During the time of the kings, it shows God's care for the nations, pointing toward his plan to bless the whole world.
summary: Jonah runs from God's call to preach to Nineveh, is swallowed by a great fish, finally obeys, and then sulks when God shows mercy to the city.

name: Micah
author: The prophet Micah from Moresheth, a village in Judah.
date: c. 740–700 BC, the same time as Isaiah.
audience: Both Israel and Judah, especially their corrupt leaders.
storyPlace: During the divided kingdom, looking ahead to a ruler born in Bethlehem who would shepherd God's people.
summary: Micah condemns injustice, foretells a coming king from Bethlehem and sums up what God asks: to act justly, love mercy and walk humbly with him.

name: Nahum
author: The prophet Nahum from Elkosh.
date: c. 660–612 BC, before Nineveh fell in 612 BC.
audience: Judah, long oppressed by the cruel Assyrian empire.
storyPlace: Late in the time of the kings, announcing the fall of Assyria, the empire that had destroyed the northern kingdom.
summary: Nahum declares that God is patient but just, and that Nineveh, Assyria's capital, will fall, which is good news for the peoples it crushed.

name: Habakkuk
author: The prophet Habakkuk.
date: c. 610–600 BC, as Babylon was rising.
audience: Judah, troubled by injustice at home and the threat of Babylon.
storyPlace: Just before the exile, a prophet questions God and learns to trust him, declaring that the righteous will live by faith.
summary: Habakkuk asks God why evil goes unpunished, is shocked by God's answer, and ends by choosing to rejoice in God even if everything else fails.

name: Zephaniah
author: The prophet Zephaniah, possibly a descendant of King Hezekiah.
date: c. 640–620 BC, during King Josiah's reign.
audience: Judah, sliding into idolatry before Josiah's reforms.
storyPlace: Late in the time of the kings, warning of the coming day of the Lord before the exile.
summary: Zephaniah warns of a great day of judgment, then pictures God rejoicing over his restored people with singing.

name: Haggai
author: The prophet Haggai.
date: 520 BC, one of the most precisely dated books.
audience: Returned exiles in Jerusalem who had stopped rebuilding the temple.
storyPlace: After the return from exile, urging the people to finish rebuilding God's house.
summary: In four short messages Haggai challenges the people to put God first, rebuild the temple and trust that its future glory will be greater.

name: Zechariah
author: The prophet Zechariah, a priest. Many scholars think chapters 9–14 were added later by other prophets.
date: Chapters 1–8 c. 520–518 BC; chapters 9–14 possibly later.
audience: Returned exiles rebuilding the temple and wondering about their future.
storyPlace: After the return from exile, looking forward to a humble king riding on a donkey and God's final reign over all the earth.
summary: Through night visions and prophecies Zechariah encourages the rebuilding and foretells a coming king, many details of which the Gospels connect with Jesus.

name: Malachi
author: Malachi, whose name means my messenger; it may be a title rather than a personal name.
date: c. 460–430 BC, around the time of Ezra and Nehemiah.
audience: The community in Judah, whose worship had become careless and half-hearted.
storyPlace: The last prophet of the Old Testament in Protestant order, followed by about 400 years of waiting for God to act again.
summary: Malachi challenges priests and people about their worship and marriages, and promises that a messenger like Elijah will prepare the way for the Lord.

name: Matthew
author: Early church tradition names Matthew, a tax collector who became one of the twelve apostles. The book itself is anonymous, and many scholars think a later Jewish Christian wrote it.
date: Probably c. 70–90 AD (some suggest the 60s). It describes Jesus' life, c. 6 BC–AD 30/33.
audience: Most likely Jewish Christians, shown how Jesus fulfils the Old Testament.
storyPlace: Opens the New Testament by connecting Jesus to Abraham and David and showing him as the promised king who brings God's kingdom.
summary: Matthew tells of Jesus' birth, teaching (including the Sermon on the Mount), miracles, death and resurrection, ending with his command to make disciples of all nations.

name: Mark
author: Early tradition names John Mark, a companion of Peter and Paul, who is said to have recorded Peter's preaching. The book itself is anonymous.
date: Probably c. 65–70 AD, likely the earliest Gospel. It describes Jesus' ministry, c. AD 27–30/33.
audience: Probably Christians in Rome, possibly facing persecution.
storyPlace: Shows Jesus as the Messiah and Son of God who brings God's kingdom and gives his life for many.
summary: The shortest Gospel moves quickly from Jesus' baptism through his healings and teaching to his suffering, death and empty tomb.

name: Luke
author: Traditionally Luke, a doctor and travel companion of Paul, who also wrote Acts. Most scholars accept that one person wrote both, though some question whether it was Luke.
date: Probably c. 70–90 AD (some suggest the early 60s). It describes c. 6 BC–AD 30/33.
audience: A man named Theophilus and a wider audience, many probably Gentile believers.
storyPlace: Shows Jesus as the Saviour for everyone, especially outsiders, and leads straight into the story of the early church in Acts.
summary: After careful research, Luke tells of Jesus' birth, his care for the poor and the lost, beloved parables like the prodigal son, and his death, resurrection and ascension.

name: John
author: Traditionally the apostle John, the beloved disciple. Some scholars think it came from a circle of his followers, built on his testimony.
date: Probably c. 90–100 AD. It describes Jesus' ministry, c. AD 27–30/33.
audience: Believers and seekers, written so that readers may believe Jesus is the Messiah and have life.
storyPlace: Begins, like Genesis, in the beginning, presenting Jesus as God's Word who became human to bring new life.
summary: John focuses on seven signs, long conversations and Jesus' I am sayings, then gives a detailed account of his last night, death and resurrection appearances.

name: Acts
author: Luke, the same writer as the Gospel of Luke.
date: Probably c. 70–90 AD (some suggest c. 62). It covers c. AD 30–62.
audience: Theophilus and the wider church, showing how the message of Jesus spread.
storyPlace: The church is born: the risen Jesus sends his Spirit and the good news spreads from Jerusalem to Rome.
summary: After Jesus ascends, the Spirit comes at Pentecost, the apostles preach, Saul becomes Paul, Gentiles are welcomed, and Paul travels the Roman world planting churches.

name: Romans
author: The apostle Paul; almost all scholars agree.
date: c. AD 57.
audience: Jewish and Gentile Christians in Rome, a church Paul had not yet visited.
storyPlace: Explains how Jesus' death and resurrection fulfil God's promise to Abraham and bring Jews and Gentiles together into one family.
summary: Paul explains that all people have sinned, that God puts people right with himself through faith in Christ, and what new life in the Spirit looks like.

name: 1 Corinthians
author: The apostle Paul; widely accepted.
audience: A gifted but divided church in the busy port city of Corinth.
storyPlace: Shows a young church learning to live as God's people, and gives one of the earliest written accounts of the resurrection.
summary: Paul tackles divisions, sexual ethics, worship, spiritual gifts and the resurrection, and includes the famous chapter on love.

name: 2 Corinthians
author: The apostle Paul. Some scholars think it combines parts of more than one letter.
audience: The church in Corinth, where some were questioning Paul's authority.
storyPlace: Part of the early church story, showing how God's power works through weakness.
summary: Paul opens his heart about his sufferings, explains the new covenant ministry of reconciliation and encourages generous giving.

name: Galatians
author: The apostle Paul; widely accepted.
date: c. AD 48–55; some scholars think it is Paul's earliest letter.
audience: Churches in Galatia (in modern Turkey), where some were telling Gentile believers to keep the Jewish law to be saved.
storyPlace: Defends the good news that Gentiles become Abraham's children through faith in Christ, a key moment in the church's growth.
summary: Paul passionately insists that people are made right with God by faith in Christ, not by the law, and that believers are free to live by the Spirit.

name: Ephesians
author: Traditionally Paul, writing from prison. Many scholars think a follower of Paul wrote it in his name.
date: c. AD 60–62 if by Paul; possibly c. 80–90.
audience: Christians in Ephesus and possibly other churches in the region.
storyPlace: Celebrates God's plan to unite everything in Christ, with Jews and Gentiles joined into one new people.
summary: Ephesians praises God for saving us by grace through faith, then shows how this new life shapes the church, the family and spiritual battles.

name: Philippians
author: The apostle Paul, writing from prison; widely accepted.
audience: The church in Philippi, a close and generous partner in Paul's work.
storyPlace: A warm thank-you letter from the early church era, showing joy in Christ even in chains.
summary: Paul thanks the Philippians, holds up Christ's humility as the pattern for our lives, and encourages them to rejoice and not be anxious.

name: Colossians
author: Traditionally Paul, writing from prison. Some scholars think a close follower wrote it.
date: c. AD 60–62 if by Paul.
audience: Christians in Colossae being drawn toward ideas that downplayed Christ.
storyPlace: Shows Christ as the one through whom everything was created and through whom God is reconciling all things.
summary: Paul declares that Christ is supreme over all creation and enough for salvation, and urges believers to set their hearts on him.

name: 1 Thessalonians
author: The apostle Paul, with Silas and Timothy; widely accepted.
date: c. AD 50–51; likely the earliest surviving New Testament writing.
audience: A young church in Thessalonica, facing opposition soon after Paul had to leave.
storyPlace: From the first years of the church's spread into Europe, looking ahead to Jesus' return.
summary: Paul encourages the new believers, urges holy living and comforts them about fellow believers who have died, promising that Christ will return.

name: 2 Thessalonians
author: Traditionally Paul. Some scholars think it was written later by a follower.
date: c. AD 51–52 if by Paul.
audience: The church in Thessalonica, confused about the day of the Lord.
storyPlace: Part of the early church story, clarifying hope about Christ's return.
summary: Paul corrects the idea that the day of the Lord has already come and tells believers to keep working faithfully while they wait.

name: 1 Timothy
author: Traditionally Paul. Many scholars think a later follower wrote it in his name.
date: c. AD 62–64 if by Paul; possibly c. 80–100.
audience: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, leading the church in Ephesus.
storyPlace: Shows the church organising itself for the long haul after the apostles' generation.
summary: Guidance on resisting false teaching, praying, choosing church leaders and caring for widows, with a charge to fight the good fight of faith.

name: 2 Timothy
author: Traditionally Paul, near the end of his life. Many scholars think a follower wrote it.
date: c. AD 64–67 if by Paul.
audience: Timothy, being encouraged to keep going.
storyPlace: Presented as Paul's farewell from prison in Rome, passing on the faith to the next generation.
summary: Paul urges Timothy not to be ashamed of the gospel, to hold on to Scripture and to keep preaching, as Paul has finished the race.

name: Titus
author: Traditionally Paul. Many scholars think a follower wrote it.
date: c. AD 62–64 if by Paul.
audience: Titus, Paul's co-worker, setting up churches on the island of Crete.
storyPlace: Part of the early church's growth, showing how God's grace trains people to live well.
summary: Paul tells Titus how to appoint leaders, teach sound doctrine and encourage good works, all grounded in God's kindness in saving us.

name: Philemon
author: The apostle Paul, writing from prison; widely accepted.
audience: Philemon, a Christian in Colossae, and the church that met in his home.
storyPlace: A small window into how the gospel reshaped relationships in the early church.
summary: Paul appeals to Philemon to welcome back his runaway slave Onesimus, now a believer, as a dear brother.

name: Hebrews
author: Unknown. Some early Christians credited Paul; others suggested Barnabas, Apollos or Priscilla. Most scholars today say we do not know.
date: Probably c. AD 60–90; many think before the temple fell in AD 70.
audience: Jewish Christians tempted to drift back from following Jesus.
storyPlace: Shows how Jesus fulfils the whole Old Testament system of priests, sacrifices and covenant.
summary: Hebrews argues that Jesus is greater than angels, Moses and the priests, that his one sacrifice is enough, and calls readers to hold on in faith like the heroes of old.

name: James
author: Traditionally James, the brother of Jesus and leader of the Jerusalem church. Some scholars think it was written later in his name.
date: c. AD 45–62 if by James; possibly later.
audience: Jewish Christians scattered abroad, many of them poor.
storyPlace: Early church teaching that echoes Jesus' Sermon on the Mount and Old Testament wisdom.
summary: James teaches that real faith shows itself in action: caring for the poor, controlling our words, resisting favouritism and enduring trials.

name: 1 Peter
author: Traditionally the apostle Peter, with help from Silas. Some scholars think it was written by his followers.
date: c. AD 62–64 if by Peter; possibly c. 70–90.
audience: Christians scattered across Asia Minor, suffering for their faith.
storyPlace: Encourages the early church to see itself as God's chosen people, strangers in the world, sharing in Christ's sufferings and glory.
summary: Peter reminds suffering believers of their living hope through Jesus' resurrection and urges them to live good, holy lives among their neighbours.

name: 2 Peter
author: Traditionally the apostle Peter. Many scholars think it was written later in his name; even some early Christians had doubts.
date: c. AD 64–68 if by Peter; many scholars suggest c. 80–120.
audience: Christians troubled by false teachers who mocked the idea of Jesus' return.
storyPlace: Looks ahead to the day of the Lord and the new heavens and new earth.
summary: Peter urges believers to grow in faith, warns against false teachers and explains that God's delay in returning is patience, not forgetfulness.

name: 1 John
author: Traditionally the apostle John. Some scholars think it came from a leader in John's community.
audience: Churches shaken after a group left them, teaching that Jesus had not truly come in the flesh.
storyPlace: From the end of the apostolic era, assuring believers of eternal life in Christ.
summary: John says that God is light and God is love, and that we know we belong to him when we trust Jesus, obey him and love one another.

name: 2 John
author: The writer calls himself the elder, traditionally the apostle John.
audience: The chosen lady and her children, probably a way of addressing a local church.
storyPlace: From the end of the apostolic era, guarding the truth about Jesus.
summary: A brief note urging believers to keep loving one another and not to welcome teachers who deny that Jesus came in the flesh.

name: 3 John
author: The elder, traditionally the apostle John.
audience: Gaius, a believer who welcomed travelling Christian teachers.
storyPlace: A glimpse of how early churches supported missionaries and dealt with difficult leaders.
summary: The elder praises Gaius for his hospitality, warns about a controlling leader named Diotrephes and commends Demetrius.

name: Jude
author: Jude, brother of James and so traditionally a brother of Jesus. Some scholars think it was written later in his name.
date: Uncertain; c. AD 60–90.
audience: Christians threatened by teachers who twisted God's grace into an excuse for immorality.
storyPlace: From the early church, urging believers to defend the faith passed down to them.
summary: Jude warns against false teachers with examples from the past and ends with a beautiful blessing to the God who keeps us from falling.

name: Revelation
author: A prophet named John, traditionally the apostle John. Since early times some have thought it was a different John.
date: Most scholars say c. AD 95, under Emperor Domitian; some suggest the late 60s.
audience: Seven churches in Asia Minor facing pressure, persecution and the pull of compromise with Rome.
storyPlace: The final chapter of the Bible's big story: Jesus wins, evil is defeated, and God makes all things new with heaven and earth joined together.
summary: Through vivid symbolic visions, John sees the risen Jesus, the heavenly throne room and the struggle between God and evil, ending with the new Jerusalem where God lives with his people.
